0.title: What Is Man?
0.essay:
Every age asks what a human being is. The answer we give shapes how we treat a newborn and a dying man, a stranger at the border and the face in the mirror.

Today’s answers

Our culture offers several answers, often at once. One says we are clever animals: products of nature, more complex than other creatures but not different in kind. Another, rarely said aloud but everywhere assumed, treats us as consumers: you are what you buy, own and choose. A third says you are a self to be expressed: look inside, find who you really are, and live it out whatever anyone says.

Each holds a grain of truth, but none can bear the weight we put on it. A clever animal has no obvious reason to lay down its life for a stranger. A consumer is only worth what he can spend. And a self that must invent its own meaning is a lonely and exhausting thing to be.

Under the night sky

Three thousand years ago David looked up at the stars and asked the question too: “When I look at your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have set in place, what is man that you are mindful of him, and the son of man that you care for him?” (Psalm 8:3–4). Yet he marvelled: “Yet you have made him a little lower than the heavenly beings and crowned him with glory and honor” (Psalm 8:5). Small, and crowned. Both are true.

Hebrews takes up the psalm and admits that we do not yet see humanity ruling as it should. “But we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus” (Hebrews 2:9). In the end the Bible answers “What is man?” with a person. This study follows that answer, from creation to glory.

The chapters

Made by God and for God; Body and Soul; Made for Each Other; The Glory Ruined; The True Man; and Crowned with Glory. The study Creation & the Fall works through Genesis 1–3; this one gathers the whole Bible’s teaching.

For reflection

Which of today’s answers (a clever animal, a consumer, a self to be expressed) shapes you most, without your noticing? And what would change if you really were “crowned … with glory and honor” (Psalm 8:5)?

1.title: Made by God and for God
1.essay:
“Know that the LORD, he is God! It is he who made us, and we are his” (Psalm 100:3). Before the Bible tells us anything else about ourselves, it tells us whose we are.

Creatures

The first thing to say about a human being is that he or she is a creature. We did not make ourselves, and we do not keep ourselves going. Paul told the philosophers of Athens that God “himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything” (Acts 17:25), and that “In him we live and move and have our being” (Acts 17:28). Every heartbeat is a gift. So Paul asks, “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

This is humbling, but also restful. God “knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust” (Psalm 103:14). He does not expect from us what only he can be.

Limits are not sin

Adam and Eve, before they ever sinned, needed food and sleep. They could be in only one place at a time. They did not know everything, and they needed each other. None of that was a flaw. Finitude is part of being a good creature in a good world.

Our age finds this hard to accept. Advertising and self-help tell us we can be anything, have everything and never stop. Then we feel guilty for being tired, for needing help, for not keeping up. Scripture is kinder and more honest: “It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep” (Psalm 127:2). Sleep is a daily confession that the world runs without us, because God does not sleep.

A young hospital doctor prided herself on never saying no. She covered every shift and answered every message, and slowly burned out. A wise older Christian showed her Psalm 127 and said, “You are trying to be God. You are only allowed to be a doctor.” She laughed, and then cried. Learning to accept her limits did not make her less useful. It made her free.

The image of God

Then comes the great word: “So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). Christians have understood this image in three main ways, and each has real strengths.

The structural view, common from the early church onwards, finds the image in what we are: our reason, our moral sense, our capacity to know God and to choose. It explains why humans alone write poetry, keep promises and pray. The relational view, developed especially in the twentieth century, finds the image in our relationships: we are made to love God and one another, as God himself is a fellowship of Father, Son and Spirit, and Genesis links the image with “male and female”. The functional or royal view, held by many Old Testament scholars, notes that ancient kings set up statues of themselves to mark their rule. Humanity is God’s living image in his world, and Genesis 1:26 joins the image directly to dominion.

This commentary’s view: these are not rivals but facets of one truth. Human beings represent and reflect God in rule, in relationship, in reason and in moral nature, and men and women bear the image equally. The fall damaged the image but did not destroy it. The study Creation & the Fall (Made in God’s Image) works through Genesis 1 itself.

Notice one thing all three views share. An image only makes sense in relation to the one it images. A mirror turned away from the light reflects nothing. We were made to face God.

The dignity of every human

Because the image belongs to being human, not to being clever, strong or useful, every human life carries dignity. After the flood God says, “Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image” (Genesis 9:6). James applies it to words: “With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God” (James 3:9). To despise a person is to insult his Maker. That dignity is not earned and cannot be lost by weakness, age or illness. It is given.

The chief end

If God made us, he made us for something. “For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be glory forever” (Romans 11:36). Paul says of Christ, “all things were created through him and for him” (Colossians 1:16). The Westminster Shorter Catechism famously answers its first question: “Man’s chief end is to glorify God, and to enjoy him forever.” Augustine said much the same in prayer: God made us for himself, and our hearts are restless until they rest in him. The study More Than You Imagined has a whole chapter on that purpose.

Here is the wonder. The God who needs nothing made creatures to share his joy. We are not raw material for his projects. We are invited into the love that the Father, Son and Spirit have always shared. Every restless longing in the human heart is, in the end, a homesickness for him.

For reflection

Where do you resent your limits, and what would it look like to accept them as a creature? Which view of the image of God had you assumed, and what do the others add? Is there anyone you speak about in a way that forgets they bear God’s likeness? How does knowing your chief end change an ordinary day?

2.title: Body and Soul
2.essay:
“The LORD God formed the man of dust from the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living creature” (Genesis 2:7). Dust and breath: a human being is both, and is one.

Neither ghost nor machine

Some ancient thinkers taught that the real you is a soul trapped in a body, longing to escape. Much modern thought says the opposite: you are only a body, and the soul is a word for what the brain does. Scripture refuses both. God did not make a body and then place a soul in it, like a driver in a car. He breathed into dust, and the result was one living person.

We do not have bodies the way we have coats. We are embodied souls, and ensouled bodies.

Two parts or three?

Christians have debated how to describe this unity. Trichotomy holds that a human has three parts: body, soul and spirit. Its defenders point to Paul’s prayer that “your whole spirit and soul and body be kept blameless” (1 Thessalonians 5:23), and to the word of God “piercing to the division of soul and of spirit” (Hebrews 4:12). Many suggest the soul is our mind and emotions, while the spirit is the part that relates to God.

Dichotomy holds that we are one person with two aspects: the material (body) and the immaterial (soul or spirit). Its defenders note that Scripture often uses soul and spirit as two names for the same thing: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior” (Luke 1:46–47) is Hebrew-style parallelism, saying one thing twice. Jesus speaks of two, not three: “do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10:28). At death “the dust returns to the earth as it was, and the spirit returns to God who gave it” (Ecclesiastes 12:7). And when Jesus calls us to love God “with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind” (Matthew 22:37), nobody thinks we have three separate organs; the words pile up to mean “all of you”. Paul’s prayer in 1 Thessalonians works the same way, and Hebrews 4 pairs soul and spirit with “joints and … marrow” to say the word cuts to the very deepest place.

A smaller number of Christians hold that a human is wholly physical, and that life after death waits entirely for the resurrection. Yet Paul says that to be “away from the body” is to be “at home with the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:8), and Jesus promised the dying thief, “today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

This commentary’s view: a human being is a unity of body and soul, with soul and spirit used interchangeably. At death the two are torn apart for a time, which is why death is an enemy, and at the resurrection they are joined again for ever.

The goodness of the body

God looked at the man and woman he had made, bodies and all, and “behold, it was very good” (Genesis 1:31). Christianity is not embarrassed by the body. The Son of God took one: “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). He rose in one, and he will raise ours. “So glorify God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:20).

That rules out two mistakes: despising the body, as if eating, sleep and touch were less spiritual than prayer, and worshipping it, as if appearance, fitness or youth were our worth. The body is neither prison nor god. It is a gift to be received with thanks and used for love.

The heart

When Scripture wants to name the centre of a person, it usually says “heart”. In the Bible the heart is not only feelings. It is where we think, choose and love: mind, will and affections together. That is why it matters so much: “Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life” (Proverbs 4:23). Jesus taught that evil comes “from within, out of the heart of man” (Mark 7:21), and that “where your treasure is, there your heart will be also” (Matthew 6:21).

This explains something about us. We do not simply do what we think is right; we do what we love most. Change that lasts must reach the heart, and only God can give a new one: “I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26).

Emotions and reason

Some Christians distrust emotions; others trust them above everything. Jesus reasoned with crowds and opponents, and he also felt deeply. At Lazarus’ tomb, “Jesus wept” (John 11:35). In Gethsemane he said, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death” (Matthew 26:38). Emotions are not a lower part of us but part of the image. Like all of us, they are fallen and must be brought under God’s truth. And reason is never neutral: our thinking follows our loves.

Because we are one, body and soul affect each other. A man in his fifties had grown flat and joyless, and he blamed his weak faith. His pastor encouraged him to see his doctor, who diagnosed depression and an underactive thyroid. Treatment, alongside the patient care of friends and the Psalms, slowly helped. If you are struggling with your mental health, see a doctor. Taking medicine is no failure of faith. The study Depression & the Christian says more.

For reflection

Do you tend to despise your body or to worship it? How does it help to know that soul and spirit name the same inner self? What does your heart love most, and how can you tell? How might care for your body be part of caring for your soul?

3.title: Made for Each Other
3.essay:
In a world God kept calling good, one thing was not: “It is not good that the man should be alone” (Genesis 2:18). Before there was any sin, there was this: we are not made to be alone.

Male and female

“Male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). The man and the woman are made in the same image, given the same blessing and the same task. Neither is more truly human. Peter tells husbands to honour their wives, “since they are heirs with you of the grace of life” (1 Peter 3:7), and Paul says, “there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28). In standing before God, in grace and in glory, men and women are equal.

Yet the difference is real and good. God gives each of us our sex through our bodies, and it is not a mistake to be overcome. This commentary holds that men and women are equal in worth and different by design, including in some callings in marriage and the church. That is gently held and carefully explained in the studies Biblical Manhood and Biblical Womanhood, and questions of sex and gender are treated with compassion in Biblical Sexuality (Male and Female He Created Them). Here it is enough to say that difference is not a threat to equality. The Father, Son and Spirit are equal in glory and distinct as persons. Unity without sameness is woven into the life of God.

Made for relationship

Why is being alone “not good”? Because we image a God who is never alone. “God is love” (1 John 4:8), and love needs someone to love. Before the world began, the Father loved the Son in the Spirit. We are made in the likeness of that fellowship, so we flourish in knowing and being known.

Marriage is the first answer to Adam’s loneliness, but not the only one. Jesus never married, and he was the most complete human being who ever lived. He had close friends, a wider circle of disciples, and a family of all who do God’s will. The Bible prizes friendship: “Two are better than one … For if they fall, one will lift up his fellow” (Ecclesiastes 4:9–10). And it gives every believer a family in the church, where “The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I have no need of you’” (1 Corinthians 12:21). The study Singleness explores this for those who are unmarried.

Our culture prizes independence. We are told that needing others is weakness. Scripture says the opposite: needing others is how we were made.

Made to work

“The LORD God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). Work came before the fall. It is not a curse, though the fall made it toil. God himself works, and we work because we bear his image.

God’s first command was a commission: “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it” (Genesis 1:28). The garden was a beginning, not an end. Humanity was to draw out the riches God had put in the world. Very early we read of the father of “all those who play the lyre and pipe” (Genesis 4:21) and of “the forger of all instruments of bronze and iron” (Genesis 4:22). Music, craft, farming, science, medicine and art all come from this calling. And at the end, “the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it” (Revelation 21:24): something of the world’s best work seems to be gathered into the new creation. The study Christian at Work takes this further.

Made to rest

And God rested. “So God blessed the seventh day and made it holy, because on it God rested from all his work that he had done in creation” (Genesis 2:3). God was not tired. He was showing us a rhythm. Israel’s Sabbath was rooted in it (Exodus 20:11), and Jesus explained its purpose: “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27).

Rest is a confession of faith. When we stop, we admit that the world does not depend on us, and that our worth does not depend on our output. The study Worship & the Lord’s Day shows how Christians keep that rhythm.

A life rebuilt

A widower in his seventies stopped going out after his wife died. His days were long and silent. A neighbour invited him to a church men’s breakfast, and someone discovered he had been a joiner. Soon he was teaching teenagers to make bird boxes on Saturday mornings and eating Sunday lunch with a young family. Nothing about his grief was fixed overnight. But he had been made for friendship, for useful work and for rest, and slowly he began to live again.

All of this is good news for people who have failed at it. Christ came into our loneliness, worked with his hands, and gives rest to the weary. He does not merely tell us how to live in community. He makes us a community, his own body.

For reflection

Where do you see equality and difference between men and women held together well? Who are the people you are “made for” in this season of life? Is your work an offering or an idol, and how can you tell? What would it look like to rest as an act of trust this week?

4.title: The Glory Ruined
4.essay:
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). The same creatures who build hospitals build gas chambers. Pascal observed that humanity is both astonishingly great and terribly wretched, and that any account of us must explain both. The Bible does.

A glory exchanged

Paul describes what went wrong. Humanity knew God but “did not honor him as God or give thanks to him” (Romans 1:21), and so “exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal man and birds and animals and creeping things” (Romans 1:23). We were made to image God. Instead we made images of our own and bowed to them.

The idols today are rarely statues. An idol is anything we look to for what only God can give: security, worth, meaning, love. Usually it is a good thing turned into an ultimate thing: a career, a marriage, children, approval, comfort, control, even our own moral record. And idols reshape their worshippers. The psalmist says of lifeless idols, “Those who make them become like them; so do all who trust in them” (Psalm 115:8). We become like what we worship. Made to reflect God’s glory, we begin to reflect the smallness of our gods.

Every part touched

Reformed Christians call this total depravity, and it is often misunderstood. It does not mean that people are as bad as they could be. Most people are not. It means that sin has reached every part of us. Think of a drop of ink in a glass of water: the water is not all ink, but none of it is untouched. Our minds are “darkened in their understanding, alienated from the life of God … due to their hardness of heart” (Ephesians 4:18). Our wills are bent. Our loves are disordered. Even our bodies age and break. And because the damage is everywhere, we cannot repair it from the inside, any more than a person can lift himself by his own collar.

The studies Creation & the Fall (The Fall) and The Doctrines of Grace (Total Depravity) set out the doctrine and its texts more fully. Here notice its realism. It explains why education and progress, good as they are, never produce good people on their own, and why the line between good and evil runs through every human heart, including our own.

Guilt and shame

The first sin brought two kinds of wound. “Then the eyes of both were opened, and they knew that they were naked” (Genesis 3:7). They covered themselves and hid. When God called, Adam answered, “I was afraid, because I was naked, and I hid myself” (Genesis 3:10).

Guilt is about what we have done: we have broken God’s law and deserve his judgment. Shame is about who we are: the sense of being exposed, unworthy and unloved. Older cultures often felt guilt keenly. Ours tends to deny guilt and is drowning in shame, managing it with fig leaves of image, achievement and curated online lives. The gospel deals with both. Christ bore our guilt on the cross, and he covers our shame. Even in Eden, before he sent them out, “the LORD God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins and clothed them” (Genesis 3:21).

Death

Sin’s last word is death. “For the wages of sin is death” (Romans 6:23). Every graveside says that something has gone wrong. Hebrews speaks of those “who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery” (Hebrews 2:15). Much human striving is a way of not thinking about it.

Marred, not erased

And yet the image remains. Genesis 9:6 and James 3:9 both speak of fallen people as made in God’s image. A human being is like a ruined cathedral: roofless and defaced, but you can still see what it was built to be, and it is still holy ground.

That is why unbelievers are so often wise, brave, kind and brilliant. God “makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good” (Matthew 5:45). He “did not leave himself without witness” (Acts 14:17). He writes “the work of the law … on their hearts” (Romans 2:15). Theologians call this common grace: God’s undeserved kindness to all, restraining evil and giving gifts of skill, beauty, conscience and love. When a non-Christian surgeon saves your life or a sceptical novelist moves you to tears, you are seeing common grace. Christians should be the first to admire it and the last to be surprised by it.

When the idol falls

An architect, not a believer, was admired for his integrity. Then a building he had poured himself into was cancelled, and he fell apart. He could not sleep. Talking it through with a Christian friend, he realised that his work had not just been his job. It had been his worth. “I didn’t know I worshipped anything,” he said. It was the beginning of a long conversation about a love that does not depend on what we achieve.

Here is the gospel’s strange comfort. We are more sinful than we ever dared believe, and more loved than we ever dared hope. Only a God who saw the whole ruin and loved us still could be trusted with our deepest secrets.

For reflection

What good thing in your life is most at risk of becoming an ultimate thing? How does the accurate meaning of total depravity differ from what you thought it meant? Do you struggle more with guilt or with shame, and how does Christ answer each? Where have you seen common grace in people who do not share your faith?

5.title: The True Man
5.essay:
“At present, we do not yet see everything in subjection to him. But we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honor because of the suffering of death” (Hebrews 2:8–9). The answer to “What is man?” is not an idea but a person.

The image of the invisible God

Adam was made in the image of God. Christ is the image of God. “He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation” (Colossians 1:15). Paul speaks of “the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God” (2 Corinthians 4:4), and of “the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4:6).

The eternal Son has always perfectly expressed the Father. When he became man, that perfect image took human form. So in Jesus we see two things at once: what God is like, and what a human being was meant to be. The study The Person & Work of Christ explains how he is fully God and fully man in one person.

Truly human

“The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). Not a costume, not an appearance: flesh. Jesus grew: he “increased in wisdom and in stature and in favor with God and man” (Luke 2:52). After fasting in the wilderness, “he was hungry” (Matthew 4:2). At a well in Samaria he sat down, “wearied as he was from his journey” (John 4:6). He wept at a friend’s grave. On the cross he said, “I thirst” (John 19:28). He “had to be made like his brothers in every respect” (Hebrews 2:17).

He was tempted too, really tempted: “one who in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). This matters. We often excuse sin by saying, “I’m only human.” But sin is not what makes us human. It is what makes us less than human. Jesus was not less human for being sinless. He was the only fully human being who has ever lived.

Humanity as it was meant to be

Watch him, and you see the image restored. He lived in glad dependence on his Father: “the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19). He used his authority to serve: “even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). He was utterly free of the need for approval, yet gentle with the broken. He enjoyed meals and children and friends. He was angry at injustice and moved by grief. Holiness in him was not grey and joyless. It was life to the full.

The last Adam

But if Jesus were only our example, he would crush us. A perfect example shows how far we fall short and gives no power to change. That is the trouble with moralism and self-help: they hand us the picture of a better human and tell us to become it.

The gospel is different. Jesus came not first as our example but as our substitute and our new head. Adam was made a living being, but “the last Adam became a life-giving spirit” (1 Corinthians 15:45). Where Adam failed, Christ obeyed. Where we deserved death, he tasted it: he was crowned “because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone” (Hebrews 2:9). And he does not hold us at arm’s length: “he is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11). The true Man went to the cross so that ruined men and women could share his life.

Renewed in the image

Joined to Christ by faith, we belong to a new humanity. Believers “have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator” (Colossians 3:10), “created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness” (Ephesians 4:24). God’s purpose is that we be “conformed to the image of his Son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8:29). The study Union with Christ explores what being “in him” means.

How does the change happen? Not mainly by staring at ourselves, but by looking at him. “And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another” (2 Corinthians 3:18). We become like what we worship, and that works for good as well as ill. Gaze at Christ, and the image is slowly restored.

A student had grown up admiring Jesus as the greatest moral teacher. The more he admired him, the more hopeless he felt. Then a friend read Hebrews 2 with him, and he saw that the Jesus he admired had tasted death for him. “I thought he was my standard,” he said. “I didn’t know he was my Saviour.” The standard did not go away. But now he had a brother who had met it for him and was changing him from within.

For reflection

Which detail of Jesus’ humanity surprises or moves you most? Have you ever used “I’m only human” as an excuse, and how does Jesus answer it? Why is Jesus as example alone bad news, and Jesus as substitute good news? What would it look like this week to “behold” his glory?

6.title: Crowned with Glory
6.essay:
“Beloved, we are God’s children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). The story of humanity does not end in ruin. It ends in glory.

Raised bodies

The Christian hope is not that we escape our bodies but that our bodies are raised. “What is sown is perishable; what is raised is imperishable. It is sown in dishonor; it is raised in glory. It is sown in weakness; it is raised in power” (1 Corinthians 15:42–43). Christ “will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body” (Philippians 3:21). The man of dust will become like the man from heaven: “we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven” (1 Corinthians 15:49).

Nothing truly human is lost; only sin and death are left behind. The study Death, Dying & Heaven looks at what happens between death and resurrection.

Reigning and seeing his face

Psalm 8 said God gave man “dominion over the works of your hands” (Psalm 8:6). In the new creation that calling is finally fulfilled, in Christ. The redeemed are made “a kingdom and priests to our God, and they shall reign on the earth” (Revelation 5:10). “They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads … and they will reign forever and ever” (Revelation 22:4–5). Creation itself waits for that day (Romans 8:19–21).

And at the centre is not our reign but his face. “As for me, I shall behold your face in righteousness; when I awake, I shall be satisfied with your likeness” (Psalm 17:15). The image will be complete when we finally see the One we image.

No ordinary people

This hope transforms how we see everyone now. C. S. Lewis wrote, “There are no ordinary people. You have never talked to a mere mortal.” The person beside you on the bus is either on the way to a glory you can hardly imagine, or to a ruin you cannot bear to think of.

So every person bears the image and deserves honour. The unborn child, whom God is knitting together “in my mother’s womb” (Psalm 139:13). The disabled, whose worth was never measured by ability. The elderly, to whom God says, “even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you” (Isaiah 46:4). The enemy: “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44). The stranger: “You shall treat the stranger who sojourns with you as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself” (Leviticus 19:34). The study Life & Death Ethics works out what this means at life’s beginning and end.

Humility and dignity together

On our own, we swing between pride and self-hatred. The gospel tells us we are more sinful than we knew, which humbles us, and more loved than we dreamed, which lifts us up. A Christian does not need to think highly of himself, nor to despise himself. He can, as Paul says, “think with sober judgment” (Romans 12:3), and then mostly forget himself in love for God and others.

Against fear and despair

This answers the two great tyrants of the human heart. The first is the fear of man: living for other people’s verdict. “The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe” (Proverbs 29:25). If God has crowned you, no human frown can uncrown you. The study The Fear of Man takes this further.

The second is despair: the sense that my life is worthless and I would be better gone. Jesus speaks straight into it: “Why, even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not; you are of more value than many sparrows” (Luke 12:7). If you are thinking about ending your life, please reach out today: call the emergency services or a crisis line, or tell someone you trust now. Your life is not your own to throw away. It was given, and it is loved.

Is he still there?

A woman visits her father, who has advanced dementia. He no longer knows her name. Some days she wonders whether he is still “there”. What holds her is this: he was made in God’s image, and that has not been withdrawn. He trusted Christ for sixty years, and Christ has not forgotten him. One day he will be raised whole, and he will know her again. So she holds his hand, sings the hymns he loved, and treats him as what he is: a man crowned with glory, waiting.

Back to the night sky

Psalm 8 begins and ends in the same place: “O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth!” (Psalm 8:9). The psalm about humanity is finally a psalm about God. That is the deepest answer to the question. We are never more truly human than when we stop gazing at ourselves and look up in wonder at the God who made us, the Son who became one of us, and the glory he will share with us for ever.

For reflection

How does the hope of a raised body change the way you think about your body now? Which group of people do you find it hardest to see as bearing God’s image? Do you tend more to pride or to self-contempt, and how does the gospel answer you? Who needs to hear from you this week that they are “of more value than many sparrows” (Luke 12:7)?
